rule: Draw dark nook-and-cranny shadows under and behind near objects to separate, define and identify them.
Overlapping is always more powerful than size for making an object look closer.
If the window or opening is on the right, its thickness is on the right; if it is on the left, the thickness is on the left.
The short peeking line at the back interior of an opening is what makes the shape read as three-dimensional.
Undershadows under overlapping parts pull the near part forward and push the part under it deeper into the picture.
Flat surfaces facing away from the light take one smooth tone; curved surfaces take blended shading from dark to light.
The upper lip dips down in the centre and the ridges under the nose line up with this dip; the lower lip is made of two round shaded forms.
In the front view vertical lines from the centre of the pupils position the corners of the lips.
The iris is a perfect circle tucked a little under the upper eyelid.
